findings.quote: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Which unit is energy measured in?
findings.what: The two warm-up questions (joules, kinetic store) are never used in this lesson, so they do not prepare her for scalars, vectors or speed. They also assume earlier lessons she may not have had.

findings.quote: Every quantity in physics has a size: a number with a unit, such as 5 kg or 20 m. The size of a quantity is also called its magnitude.
findings.what: 'Quantity' is used without saying it means something you can measure. The exam word 'magnitude' is introduced here and never used again, so it will not stick.

findings.quote: A push of 10 newtons to the left does not do the same as 10 newtons to the right.
findings.what: Force and the newton are used as the example for a vector here, but a force is not explained until 6.1, the last key point. She only meets 'newtons measure force' if she got 1.1a wrong.

findings.quote: In a straight line from your start, you are 500 m away, about 53° north of east.
findings.what: The 500 m and the 53° appear from nowhere. She will not see how 300 m and 400 m give 500 m, because nothing mentions the right-angled triangle or Pythagoras, and there is no picture in the script.

findings.quote: The straight-line distance from start to finish, with its direction, is called the displacement.
findings.what: The lesson never says that displacement is a vector, though 1.6 says distance is a scalar. The scalar/vector pairing, which is the point of this key point, is left unfinished.

findings.quote: Velocity is speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector.
findings.what: The lesson file's 'velocity = displacement ÷ time' is never taught, yet the key point is treated as complete.

findings.quote: Yes: the speed stays the same, but the direction changes all the way round.
findings.what: Her correct answer begins 'No: the direction keeps changing' and the reply begins 'Yes:'. The reply does not fit the answer it follows and reads oddly.

findings.quote: Yes: your line makes every point. You have this: a scalar has a size only. You have this: a vector has a size and a direction.
findings.what: The feedback on her own-words line is a stilted template that repeats 'You have this:'. It does not read like a teacher responding to what she wrote, and the same pattern recurs at 2.16, 3.12, 4.7, 5.11 and 6.9.

findings.quote: The equation is s = v t: distance travelled = speed × time.
findings.what: The lesson file gives v = d/t with d for distance; the script uses s instead. It also defines average speed as distance ÷ time in 2.1 and then presents the equation in the multiplied form, so the equation does not match the sentence she has just read.

findings.quote: Here s is the distance in metres (m), v is the speed in metres per second (m/s) and t is the time in seconds (s).
findings.what: In one sentence 's' is both the symbol for distance and the unit symbol for seconds. A first-time learner will very likely mix the two up.

findings.quote: Not quite: 8 m/s. You multiplied. Speed is distance divided by time: 1000 ÷ 125 = 8 m/s.
findings.what: On every typed-number question a wrong answer is met with the right answer straight away. She never gets a hint and a second try, so she does not get to correct her own mistake.

findings.quote: A train travels 3 km in 100 s. What is its average speed, in m/s?
findings.what: Converting kilometres to metres has not been mentioned before this question; it is taught only in the feedback after she slips up.

findings.quote: Walking is about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. Sound travels through air at about 330 m/s.
findings.what: Four numbers to remember in one message, and only walking is used afterwards. The lesson file's motorway car and speed of light are left out.

findings.quote: A distance-time graph shows how far something has gone at each moment. Time runs along the bottom and distance goes up the side.
findings.what: Graphs are taught entirely in words from 2.9 to 2.15, and again at 3.8 to 3.10. Nothing in the script shows her a graph, and a first-time learner cannot picture flat, sloping and curved lines from sentences alone.

findings.quote: How steep a line is, found from how far it rises divided by how far it runs along, is called the gradient.
findings.what: This is a tangled sentence for a 15-year-old, with the new word arriving at the very end after two nested clauses. It should say plainly that the gradient is how steep the line is, then how to find it.

findings.quote: That line is a tangent, and its gradient is the speed at that moment.
findings.what: Tangents are not in the lesson file's key point 2. A new term and method are added by the script and never practised or checked.

findings.quote: Partly there. You have this: it gives the speed. Still needed: steeper means faster.
findings.what: The question asks what the gradient tells you, and 'the speed' is a complete answer. Telling her she is only 'partly there' is unfair marking.

findings.quote: Here is what a good line says. It gives the speed. Steeper means faster.
findings.what: 'It' has no referent in the message; the gradient is not named.

findings.quote: Here a is the acceleration in metres per second squared (m/s²)
findings.what: The unit m/s² is given with no explanation that it means metres per second gained each second. To a first-time learner a 'squared second' is baffling.

findings.quote: The change in velocity is 8 − 2 = 6 m/s, so the deceleration is 6 ÷ 3 = 2 m/s².
findings.what: 3.3 said the change is final minus starting velocity and 3.6 said it is negative when slowing, yet every branch here works out starting minus final and calls +6 the change. By the lesson's own rule the change is 2 − 8 = −6 m/s, and the size is then 2 m/s².

findings.quote: A velocity-time graph has velocity up the side and time along the bottom. Its gradient is the acceleration. A flat line means a steady velocity, with no acceleration.
findings.what: Three ideas arrive in one message: a new graph, what its gradient means and what a flat line means. None is built up or pictured.

findings.quote: The area under a velocity-time graph is the distance travelled. A straight line rising from zero makes a triangle, with area = ½ × base × height.
findings.what: 'The area under a graph' is not explained (between the line and the time axis), nor why an area should be a distance. 'A straight line … makes a triangle' is not clear without a picture.

findings.quote: Partly there. You have this: how quickly the velocity changes. Still needed: the change in velocity divided by the time.
findings.what: 'How quickly the velocity changes' is exactly the definition taught in 3.1 and fully answers 'what is acceleration?'. Marking it as only partly right is unfair.

findings.quote: Here is what a good line says. How quickly the velocity changes. The change in velocity divided by the time.
findings.what: The model answer is two sentence fragments with no subject. It is not a good line she could copy.

findings.quote: The equation is v² − u² = 2 a s
findings.what: The lesson file's key point 4 has three equations (v = u + at, s = ½(u + v)t, v² = u² + 2as). The script teaches only one, in a different form, and then counts the key point as taught.

findings.quote: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
findings.what: This is a second worked example on the same equation with the identical introduction. It does not say it is another one or what is different (finding a, with braking).

findings.quote: Not quite: 1 m/s². Square each velocity first: 6² − 4² = 36 − 16 = 20.
findings.what: An answer of 0.2 comes from (6 − 4) ÷ 10, which misses both the squaring and the factor of 2. The feedback names only the squaring.

findings.quote: Partly there. You have this: final velocity squared minus starting velocity squared. Still needed: equals 2 × acceleration × distance.
findings.what: The two marking 'points' are the two halves of one equation, so the feedback reads as broken fragments. The 'none' branch ('Final velocity squared minus starting velocity squared. Equals 2 × acceleration × distance.') is worse.

findings.quote: the velocity changes by the same amount every second, so its graph has no bends.
findings.what: It does not say which graph, and 'has no bends' is vague. It should say the velocity-time graph is a straight line.

findings.quote: Some things fall with only their weight acting on them: there is no air resistance. Falling under gravity alone is called free fall.
findings.what: 'Weight' as a force, 'air resistance' and 'free fall' all arrive in one message. Weight is never explained as the pull of gravity, and here it is swapped with 'gravity' as if she already knew they are the same thing.

findings.quote: With no air, a hammer and a feather are dropped together from the same height. Which lands first?
findings.what: The message just before (5.4) said 'Its mass makes no difference', which is the answer.

findings.quote: The up and down forces are then equal, so the object stops speeding up.
findings.what: Why equal forces mean a steady speed rather than stopping is asserted, not explained. This is her first lesson on forces, and most pupils expect balanced forces to mean 'not moving'.

findings.quote: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. Which is true of the forces on the skydiver?
findings.what: 5.7 has just said the air resistance grows 'until it is as big as the weight' and 'the up and down forces are then equal'. The answer is in the message before.

findings.quote: When the parachute opens, the air resistance jumps up and becomes bigger than the weight.
findings.what: 'The parachute' has not been mentioned. The skydiver appeared only in the previous question, so this message does not stand on its own.

findings.quote: Why does it stop speeding up?
findings.what: The right option, 'Air resistance grows until it equals the weight', is 5.7 almost word for word and was already the answer to 5.8. She is asked the same thing twice within three steps.

findings.quote: Here is what a good line says. Air resistance increases with speed. Until it equals the weight.
findings.what: 'Until it equals the weight.' is a fragment. The model line is not a proper sentence.

findings.quote: A force between objects that are touching is called a contact force. Friction, air resistance and the tension in a rope are contact forces.
findings.what: 'Contact force', 'friction' and 'tension' are all new in one message. Friction and tension are not explained at all.

findings.quote: Gravity, magnetic force and electrostatic force are examples.
findings.what: 'Electrostatic force' is used with no explanation; she will not know what it is.

findings.quote: Which of these is a contact force?
findings.what: 6.2 listed 'the tension in a rope' as a contact force and 6.4 listed gravity and magnetic force as non-contact, immediately before. She only has to read the lists back.

findings.quote: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson.
findings.what: The quiz has no question on key point 4 (the equation of motion), while key point 3 gets two. It is not on the whole lesson.

findings.quote: which is true when a falling object reaches terminal velocity?
findings.what: This is the third time the same question, with the same answer 'air resistance equals the weight', has been asked (5.8, 5.10, 6.15). The fact has also been stated in 5.7, 5.9 and 5.11.

findings.quote: V² − u² = 2 a s: final velocity squared minus starting velocity squared equals 2 × acceleration × distance.
findings.what: The equation is written with a capital V. The symbol is lower-case v, and V means something else in physics (potential difference, volume).

findings.quote: Button: Next
findings.what: There is nothing hands-on anywhere in the script: no graph to draw or drag, no motion to try, no measuring a speed. Every step is read, tap Next, or answer a question.

findings.quote: Forces and motion — speed, velocity and acceleration: the scripted AI lesson (key points 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
findings.what: Six key points, about eighty steps, four equations and two kinds of graph in one sitting is far too much for a first meeting. With no pictures or activity she is likely to switch off well before the forces section.

overall: No, not as it is. The physics is mostly sound and the wrong-answer replies are generally well aimed, but several things would mislead a first-time learner: 's' used for distance beside '(s)' for seconds, the 500 m and 53° that come from nowhere, the deceleration working that contradicts the lesson's own 'final minus starting' rule, weight and air resistance used as forces before force is taught, and graphs taught wholly in words with no picture in the script. The terminal-velocity questions and the hammer-and-feather question are answered by the message before them, and the own-words marking calls complete answers 'partly there'. I would fix those and split it into shorter sittings with something hands-on, since six key points in one unbroken run is too much.
